paras: The lynching of Mitchell Gilbert took place near Cordele, Georgia, during the night of October 15–16, 1903, when a Black former farm hand was hanged from a tree beside a public road south of the town and his body riddled with bullets. Wire reports carried across the country described him only as "an unknown negro" and said neither the cause nor the killers were known, while a Georgia paper named him and reported that a posse had hanged him for writing a letter to a young woman. The Black weekly St. Paul Appeal cited the case as "the latest from Lynchland" and called it murder.

According to the Savannah Morning News, Gilbert had worked as a farm hand on the place of C. C. Green until about three weeks before his death and had not been seen since. The Americus Times-Recorder, citing "parties from Dooly county" who came to Americus on October 16, reported that Gilbert had written a letter to "one of the best known young ladies of that section." She gave the letter to her father, who, in the paper's words, "ferreted out the matter and fixed the guilt upon Mitchell Gilbert." Its contents and the woman's race went unstated, though the subhead called it an "insult."

In the account the Times-Recorder printed, a posse found Gilbert a few miles from town, hanged him from a tree and filled his body with bullets. Neighbors later said they had heard shots in the night but had not investigated. The body was found still hanging on the morning of October 16.

The Savannah Morning News placed it two miles south of Cordele on the Wenona public road; other reports said one mile or two and a half miles. The Constitution described the dead man as about 25 years old and said the body was "riddled with pistol shots."

A "jury of investigation" looked into the death, but according to the Savannah Morning News the cause of the hanging was not known to it or to anyone else. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

Papers outside Georgia learned of the killing through an Associated Press dispatch dated at Cordele on October 16, which called the dead man "an unknown negro" and said investigation had not established his identity. Versions of it ran on October 16 and 17 in the Deseret Evening News, the Richmond Times-Dispatch, the Raleigh News & Observer, the Indianapolis Journal and the Washington Times, under headlines such as "Negro Lynched," "Negroe Hung and Filled with Bullets" and "Georgia Negro Hanged." Weeklies such as the Kingstree, South Carolina, County Record and the Sharp County Record carried it as a brief the following week.

The Americus Times-Recorder printed the wire on its front page on October 17 as an Atlanta Journal special, and on an inside page the same day gave Gilbert's name and the letter story under the headline "Lynched for Writing Letter" and the subhead "Negro Offers an Insult and Pays the Penalty." That item, which came secondhand from Dooly county visitors and told the killing as a penalty paid ("promptly strung up to the first real good tree"), was reprinted with credit by the Savannah Morning News on October 19 and without credit by the Dawson News on October 21.

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal of October 24 quoted the wire as "the latest from Lynchland" and argued that if the man "had committed a crime," the daily press, "ever ready to show the bad side of the race," would have said so. The Appeal concluded that the killing was a case of "murder pure and simple, without any extenating circumstances whatever," and it repeated the paragraph in its October 31 issue. Working from the wire alone, it did not name Gilbert or mention the letter.

The Savannah Morning News's Cordele dispatch said the cause was unknown to anyone, including the jury of investigation, while the Americus Times-Recorder attributed the killing to the letter on the word of unnamed Dooly county visitors, an account that gives only the lynchers' side. No later report in the coverage settled which version was correct.

reader.title: Lynching of Mitchell Gilbert
bases: A Black man was found hanged and shot near Cordele, which the papers headlined as a lynching (A1, A3, A9); one local account says a posse hanged and shot him over a letter (A4).

Gilbert was hanged and his body riddled with bullets with no legal process (A2, A5, A9); the Americus account attributes the killing to a posse punishing him for a letter to a young lady (A4), and the wire and Atlanta reports call it a lynching (A3, A9), though no number of men is given.

The AP/Journal wire (A2, A3), the Savannah Morning News Cordele dispatch (A5) and the Atlanta Constitution special (A9) independently agree that a Black man's hanged and bullet-riddled body was found near Cordele on Oct. 16; the cause rests on one secondhand account (A4).

framing.detail: National papers ran the brief AP wire under heads such as 'Negro Lynched', 'Negroe Hung and Filled with Bullets' and 'Georgia Negro Hanged', naming no victim and no cause.

The Americus Times-Recorder headed the posse account 'Lynched for Writing Letter / Negro Offers an Insult and Pays the Penalty' and told the hanging without criticism ('promptly strung up to the first real good tree').
The Savannah Morning News and Atlanta Constitution reported the cause and lynchers as unknown without comment.
The St. Paul Appeal listed it as 'the latest from Lynchland' and read the press's silence about any crime as evidence of murder pure and simple.
